abstract: Philosophers and psychologists distinguish many forms of self, yet neuroimaging results often implicate a shared core in the cortical midline or insula. We propose self-related processing arises from shifting coalitions of distributed brain systems, without a core. In a meta-analysis of 912 neuroimaging publications, titles and abstracts clustered into ten forms, including autobiographical memory, body ownership and interoception. No single location was significant in all ten associated brain maps, although each occupied different parts and amounts of midline and insular territory. Their differences were distributed across the brain. Regional patterns varied with study context, corresponded selectively with aspects of consciousness and resembled maps of general functions. Brain patterns combined at continuously varying strengths predicted regions reported in held-out publications better than single patterns or on/off combinations. Self-related processing therefore has no core and arises from shifting coalitions of distributed brain systems whose graded contributions define a continuous configuration space.
